Two parameters deviate in their rank mean. For

the rank mean of 544 lies 3.4 standard errors above the expected value, which means that the true value falls in the upper part of the posterior more often than calibration allows, that is, the posterior of
is shifted downward relative to the true value. This is the direction expected from the boundary effect described in
, because posteriors of values near the upper bound of 1.0 cannot extend above the bound. For

the rank mean of 467 lies 2.5 standard errors below the expected value, so that its posterior is shifted upward relative to the true value. A corresponding boundary effect at the lower bound of 0 is a candidate explanation, but it has not been checked, and the earlier description of
as free of boundary effects does not hold for the current network.
The rank standard deviation exceeds its expected value for five of the six parameters, by 1.1 to 1.7 standard errors for four of them and by 3.0 standard errors for
. A rank standard deviation above the expected value arises when true values fall in the tails of the posterior too often, that is, when posteriors are somewhat too narrow. For

the posterior is therefore unbiased on average, but its width is, on this evidence, slightly underestimated, and the statement that its limited point recovery is fully reflected in appropriately wide credible intervals has to be qualified accordingly.

Rank means and standard deviations summarise only the first two moments of the rank distribution and do not locate a deviation within the parameter range. The rank histograms in the figure, and preferably empirical cumulative distribution function difference plots with simultaneous confidence bands (
), are needed to decide whether the deviations of
are confined to the bounds and whether the excess rank dispersion of
is reliable. Both are open items.

Because the correlation is computed over the full prior range, it describes recovery across that range and not specifically in the region occupied by participants.
